title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the exact degree, the second fact, and the comparison that hides

questions.prompt: A warning painted on the wall of a reservoir near Bizerte reads: "The ice on this water is never thick enough to walk on." The town wants the same warning on a metal sign, but written with the adjective THIN. Which line says exactly the same thing?

options.text: The ice on this water is never too thin to walk on.
The ice on this water is always too thin to walk on.
The ice on this water is always thin enough to walk on.
The ice on this water is never thin enough to walk on.

questions.explanation: "The ice on this water is always too thin to walk on." carries the original warning across. Turning a not enough sentence into a too sentence takes three changes at once, and they travel together: the adjective becomes its opposite, enough becomes too, and the negative moves out of the sentence, because too ... to already carries it. Never thick enough therefore becomes always too thin. "The ice on this water is never thin enough to walk on." changes the adjective and nothing else, and the result says the ice is never sufficiently thin, that is, always thick: the sign would send people onto the water. "The ice on this water is never too thin to walk on." says the ice always bears a walker, the exact reverse of the warning. And "The ice on this water is always thin enough to walk on." is worse still, since adjective + enough + to states that the action does take place.

questions.prompt: Rania wants the first line of her report on the new treatment plant to open on the words "Not only". Her two facts: the plant purifies the town's waste water, and it sells the treated water to three farms. Which opening is correct English?

options.text: Not only the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms.
Not only the plant does purify the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms.
Not only does the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms.
Not only does the plant purify the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms.

questions.explanation: "Not only does the plant purify the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms." is the correct opening. When a sentence begins with Not only, English inverts the auxiliary and the subject exactly as it does in a question; the verb purify has no auxiliary of its own, so does appears and takes the tense, leaving the main verb in the bare form. "Not only the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms." leaves the word order of an ordinary statement, and a sentence-initial Not only never allows that. "Not only does the plant purifies the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms." brings in does but marks the tense twice, on the auxiliary and on the verb; after does the verb keeps its bare form. And "Not only the plant does purify the town's waste water, but it also sells it to three farms." puts does after the subject instead of before it, which is emphasis, not inversion.

questions.prompt: A leaflet from the water company contains this line: "Farming accounts for about 80 % of the country's water consumption." A pupil has to pass the same information on without using the phrase "accounts for". Which rewrite keeps the meaning?

options.text: Farming uses about 80 % of the country's water.
Farming explains why the country's water consumption is so high.
Farming pays for about 80 % of the country's water.
Farming keeps an account of the country's water consumption.

questions.explanation: "Farming uses about 80 % of the country's water." is the rewrite. To account for a share of a total means to be that share of it, and consumption is the amount used up, so the leaflet is saying that farming is the user of four fifths of the water. "Farming explains why the country's water consumption is so high." takes the other meaning of account for, to give the reason for something; the leaflet gives a proportion, not an explanation, and a share and a cause are not the same claim. "Farming pays for about 80 % of the country's water." reads the word account as money, the trap the noun sets for anybody translating word by word. And "Farming keeps an account of the country's water consumption." turns farming into a bookkeeper: to keep an account of something is to record it, which is what a meter does, not what a farm does.

questions.prompt: A caretaker in Sfax had written this notice: "Not only the tank but also the pipes are leaking." He then decides to name the tank second, because it is the more serious of the two problems. What must his new notice say?

options.text: Not only the pipes but also the tank are leaking.
Not only the pipes but also the tank is leaking.
Not only the pipes but also the tank were leaking.
Not only the pipes but also the tank, they are leaking.

questions.explanation: "Not only the pipes but also the tank is leaking." is the new notice. When not only and but also join two subjects, the verb agrees with the NEARER one, the one that follows but also; the caretaker has moved the singular tank into that position, so are has to become is. "Not only the pipes but also the tank are leaking." keeps the plural verb of the first notice and makes it agree with the pipes, which now stand furthest from the verb: it is the commonest mistake with this structure. "Not only the pipes but also the tank were leaking." changes the tense instead of the agreement, and a notice about a leak that is being repaired describes the present, not the past. And "Not only the pipes but also the tank, they are leaking." adds a pronoun that repeats the subject already there; English builds this structure with one subject group and one verb.

questions.prompt: Emna is writing the last line of her article on the old aqueduct above the valley. She wants to say that the aqueduct carried the life of the town, and she wants to say it WITHOUT announcing that she is comparing. Which line is the metaphor she is looking for?

options.text: The aqueduct was like a vein running under the fields.
The aqueduct was as necessary to the town as a vein.
The aqueduct was the vein of the town.
The aqueduct complained under the weight of the water.

questions.explanation: "The aqueduct was the vein of the town." is the metaphor: it states the comparison as a fact, with no like and no as, and leaves the reader to work out in what way an aqueduct is a vein. That silence is exactly what Emna asked for. "The aqueduct was like a vein running under the fields." announces the comparison with like, which is the sign of a simile. "The aqueduct was as necessary to the town as a vein." announces it with the other sign, as ... as, so it is a simile too, and it even names the point of comparison, which is the opposite of saying nothing. And "The aqueduct complained under the weight of the water." gives a human action to a thing, which is a personification, the third name your book offers and a different figure from the one she wants.

questions.prompt: Your grammar summary opens its entry on adverbs of degree with this rule: an adverb of degree modifies an adjective OR another adverb, and stands in front of it. In which of these four lines does the adverb of degree modify another ADVERB?

options.text: The tap in the yard was quite loose.
The lorry was too heavy for the old bridge.
The guide was very friendly.
The volunteers worked extremely carefully.

questions.explanation: "The volunteers worked extremely carefully." is the line: carefully answers the question HOW they worked, so it is an adverb, and extremely stands in front of it to say how much. In "The tap in the yard was quite loose." the word after quite is loose, which tells you what the tap WAS, not how anything was done, so it is an adjective. "The lorry was too heavy for the old bridge." works the same way: heavy describes the lorry itself. And "The guide was very friendly." is the trap of the set: friendly ends in -ly, which usually marks an adverb, but here it follows was and describes the guide, so it is an adjective, exactly like lovely, lonely and daily in the same position.
